title: microburst-latency-cost-cpm-bench-notes
content:
Purpose and scope:

These are working notes from a short spike looking at microburst traffic patterns (many small requests, median seq_len 8–32 tokens) and their effect on latency and cost-per-million-tokens (CPM) across hardware and config axes. Goal: produce a small set of collateral (1-pager + ASCII charts) we can reuse in sales/solutions conversations to show how runtime knobs (batching, prefix/KV caching, quantization, fallback routing) change unit economics for interactive microbursts.

Summary (TL;DR):
- Microbursts hurt throughput efficiency: continuous batching overheads and kernel launch costs dominate when requests are tiny.
- KV/prefix caching + smaller-seq optimized kernels reduce p95 by ~25–45% and reduce inferred CPM by ~15–35% for representative workloads.
- Int8 quantization gives best CPM but can increase p95 tail in worst cases unless paired with fallback to fp16 for long sequences.
- Smart routing to CPU-backed small-model variants for <64-token requests can be cheaper overall if cost-of-failure (latency SLO) is acceptable.

Setup and workload profile:
- Models tested: open-llama-13b-int8 (quantized), redwood-7b-fp16, redwood-13b-fp16 (baseline), redwood-13b-int8 (quantized).
- Hardware: A100-80GB, H100-80GB, T4 (midsized), and a CPU instance (48 vCPU) as reference fallback.
- Workload: Poisson arrival bursts (lambda 50 req/s average, instantaneous spikes up to 300 req/s), request tokens: uniformly sampled in {8, 16, 32} (75% of traffic) and {128, 256} (25% of traffic).
- Latency SLO targets: p95 < 200ms for interactive features, p50 < 40ms.
- Cost metric: CPM = cost to serve 1,000,000 output tokens (USD) including infra amortized and inferred electricity/infra per hour. Note: absolute $ numbers are for internal discussion only (do not share externally).

Key experiment configs:
1) base: no caching, conservative batching (max_batch 32, max_wait 10ms), fp16, A100.
2) cache-enabled: prefix/KV cache with 60s TTL, same batching.
3) aggressive-batching: max_batch 128, max_wait 40ms (good for throughput but increases avg latency).
4) quantized: int8 kernels + cache.
5) smart-route: route <=64 token requests to redwood-7b on T4/CPU if latency predicted < SLO.

Representative numeric results (rounded):
- Base (13b fp16, A100): p50 36ms, p95 210ms, throughput during bursts 450 tok/s, CPM = $82.
- Cache-enabled (13b fp16, A100): p50 28ms, p95 145ms, throughput 720 tok/s, CPM = $62 (−24%).
- Aggressive-batching (13b fp16, A100): p50 55ms, p95 260ms, throughput 1.2k tok/s, CPM = $49 (−40%) but p95 misses SLO.
- Quantized (13b int8, H100): p50 30ms, p95 165ms, throughput 900 tok/s, CPM = $44 (−46% vs base).
- Smart-route (<=64 tok -> 7b on T4): weighted p50 22ms, p95 155ms, throughput combined 850 tok/s, CPM = $38 (−54%).

Interpretation notes:
- Aggressive batching improves CPM but increases tail latency significantly. For interactive features we can’t trade off p95 for lower cost unless UI tolerates delay.
- Cache impact is disproportionately large for microbursts because repeated prefixes occur frequently (chat continuations, system prompts). Even a modest TTL (30–60s) captured many duplicates.
- Int8 helps cost but must be validated: in ~3% of sampled prompts we saw subtle degenerations in token distribution (repetition) — opened GH-PR-9812 to add a quick A/B toggle per-customer and add a regression alert linked to evaluation prompts.

   - Agg-batch   (260ms, $49)

Actionable recommendations (short):
- Default for interactive microburst workloads: enable prefix/KV caching + conservative batching (max_wait 10–20ms). This gives good latency and ~20–30% cost savings.
- Offer quantization as an opt-in for customers with strict cost targets; pair with evals and quick rollback. Add a fallback to fp16 if hallucination/degeneration signals trigger.
- Provide a prebuilt smart-route policy template in Console: "burst-tiling-small-requests" that routes <=64-token requests to smaller model pool with graceful fallback and sharding rules. Include expected CPM and p95 ranges.
- For throughput-focused customers (batching-friendly UIs or bulk transforms), a separate preset that increases max_batch and max_wait can be recommended — note explicit p95 regression and call that out in docs.

Open questions / next spikes:
- Quantize+cache edgecases: when cache hit + int8 happens, we saw occasional micro-stalls tied to kernel fusion fallback. Need kernel-level tracing (SRE/infra). (JIRA INF-452)
- Cost accounting: current CPM includes amortized GPU-hour price but not rack-level networking egress costs. We should expand to a model that includes multi-region routing cost for customers who need global fallback.
- Better synthetic workload: our Poisson+bursts is ok but we should replay sampled real traffic from two customers (with consent) to capture diurnal patterns.

Notes for slides/pitch copy (short bullets):
- "Microbursts are common for chat UIs — without caching they can cost 20–50% more per token."
- "Enabling KV caching and lightweight routing cuts p95 and CPM with no model change."
- "Int8 is the best lever for pure cost reduction but must be paired with evaluation and per-customer rollbacks."

Appendix: quick methodological notes
- Each measurement is median of 5 runs of the burst simulation (10 minutes each) to reduce variance.
- Costs projected from cloud list prices + internal enterprise discounts; treat as indicative.
- For reproducibility see linked artifacts: CONFLUENCE-1234 (experiment notebook), GH-PR-9812 (quantize gate), JIRA-INF-452 (kernel trace request).

Raw sample trace (short):
- time 10:03:12.112 GET /generate id=abc123 seq_len=16 -> queued 3ms -> exec 22ms -> response 41ms (hit cache)
- time 10:03:12.128 POST /generate id=def456 seq_len=8 -> queued 9ms -> exec 28ms -> response 52ms (cache miss)
- time 10:03:12.129 POST /generate id=ghi789 seq_len=256 -> queued 1ms -> exec 310ms -> response 325ms (long seq)
